h: Prime ministers, a niece with green fingers and Caesar's beach
p: Walmer was one of a trio of forts Henry VIII built along this stretch of coast around 1539 and 1540, alongside Deal Castle and Sandown Castle. Sandown has largely been lost to the sea, but Walmer and Deal still stand, and seeing both in one day is a real treat. Deal Castle's shape, like a Tudor rose from above, makes a great contrast with how Walmer was later turned into a home.

Wellington isn't the only big name in the guest book. William Pitt the Younger lived here as Lord Warden during the Napoleonic Wars, when invasion felt like a very real threat, and his niece, Lady Hester Stanhope, helped lay out early parts of the gardens. Winston Churchill was Lord Warden too, and the Queen Mother held the post for over twenty years, staying here regularly.

Here's another bit of history right on the doorstep. The beach between Walmer and Deal is traditionally thought to be where Julius Caesar landed in 55 BC, and there's a memorial on the seafront marking the tradition.
Allow two to three hours for the castle and gardens. The walk along the front into Deal is flat and easy, with sea views all the way.

Make it a weekend and you can add Dover Castle and the White Cliffs, a short drive south, or the medieval streets of Sandwich, just up the coast. The cliffs at Kingsdown, south of Walmer, are a cracking spot for a breezy walk too.
